claude_fable_5.1_high/001: **Strategy:** This is misère Nim (the player taking the last object loses). The winning theory: if at least one pile has size ≥ 2, the position is losing for the player to move iff the XOR (nim-sum) of all piles is 0 — exactly as in normal Nim. If all piles are 0 or 1, the position is losing for the player to move iff the number of 1-piles is odd. My policy enumerates every legal move, evaluates the resulting position with this rule, and returns any move that leaves the opponent in a losing position. If no such move exists (we're already in a losing position), it plays a safe stalling move (take 1 from the largest pile) to prolong the game and give the opponent room to err. A legal move is always guaranteed.
claude_fable_5.1_high/002:
**Strategy:** This is misère Nim (taking the last object loses). Perfect play:
- If at least two piles have size ≥ 2, play standard Nim: move so the XOR of all piles becomes 0 (a normal-Nim winning move never collapses all piles to ≤1 when two big piles exist, so misère is irrelevant here). If the XOR is already 0 (losing position), make a small stalling move (take 1 from the largest pile) to give the opponent chances to err.
- If exactly one pile has size ≥ 2, we control the endgame: reduce that pile to 0 or 1 so that the number of 1-piles left is odd (opponent is forced to take the last object).
- If all piles are ≤ 1: take a single 1 (only possible move); we win if the count of ones is even.
A fallback always guarantees a legal move.
claude_fable_5.1_high/003:
**Strategy:** This is misère Nim (last to take loses). Optimal play follows the classic misère theory:

1. If at least two piles have size > 1, play like normal Nim: move to a position with XOR (nim-sum) zero. If already zero (losing position), make a small "stalling" move (take 1 from the largest pile) to maximize the opponent's chances of erring.
2. If exactly one pile has size > 1, reduce it to 0 or 1 so that an odd number of 1-piles remain — the opponent is then forced to take the last object.
3. If all piles are ≤ 1, the only option is taking a single object from a non-empty pile.

Every branch returns a legal `'pile,take'` string, with a guarded fallback.
claude_fable_5.1_high/004:
**Strategy:** This is misère Nim (taking the last object loses). Optimal play is the standard misère Nim rule:

1. If at least two piles have size ≥ 2, play exactly like normal Nim: make the XOR (nim-sum) of all piles zero. Such a move can never leave a position with only one big pile, so it's safe.
2. If exactly one pile has size ≥ 2, reduce it to 0 or 1 so that the number of piles equal to 1 is odd — this forces the opponent to take the last object.
3. If all piles are 0 or 1, just take one object (we win iff the count of 1s is even).
4. If the position is losing (XOR is zero with ≥2 big piles), make a "stalling" move (take 1 from the largest pile) to give the opponent maximum chance to err.

Always returns a legal move.
claude_fable_5.1_high/005: **Strategy:** This is misère Nim (taking the last object loses). The optimal theory: if any pile has size ≥ 2, play like normal Nim (move to XOR = 0), except when the move would leave all piles ≤ 1 — in that case leave an *odd* number of 1-piles. If all piles are already ≤ 1, the only choice is to take a single object; the position is won iff the number of 1-piles is even. My policy enumerates every legal move, evaluates the resulting position with this exact misère rule (P-position ⇔ [all ≤ 1 and odd count of ones] or [some pile ≥ 2 and XOR = 0]), and picks a winning move whenever one exists. If the position is already lost, it falls back to a stalling heuristic (take 1 from the largest pile) to maximize the chance the opponent errs. A legal move is always returned.
